questions.q: What makes an application a monolith?
questions.explain: A monolith is about deployment and runtime: one unit. It can be, and should be, well structured inside. "Hard to change" describes a badly structured codebase of any architecture.
options: It is written in one file
It has no layers or folders
All its features are built, deployed and run as one program, usually with one database
It is old and hard to change

questions.q: ShopFlow has three developers and eight weeks. Why is a monolith the right first architecture?
questions.explain: Early on, the biggest risk is building the wrong thing, and boundaries drawn too early are drawn wrong. A monolith keeps every change cheap. It can be given hard boundaries later, and parts extracted when a real reason appears.
options: It gives one transaction across areas, function calls instead of network calls, one deploy and cheap refactoring, while the team is still learning where the business boundaries are
Because it can never be split later

questions.q: Stock and orders live in two separate systems. What does this print?
questions.explain: The first change happened and the second did not, and nothing undid the first. Two bags are gone with no order. One database transaction makes both changes happen together or not at all.
options:
checkout failed: orders system unreachable
rice in stock: 1 orders: 0

checkout failed: orders system unreachable
rice in stock: 3 orders: 0

checkout failed: orders system unreachable
rice in stock: 3 orders: 1

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The second update would make the stock -1, so the CHECK refuses it (code 23514, check violation). The transaction rolls back, and the first update is undone too: the stock is 3 again.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The foreign key makes the database refuse an order for a user who does not exist (23503, foreign key violation). In one shared database, such rules between areas come for free; across services, you have to check them yourself.
options:
order for user 1 saved
order for user 42 saved

questions.q: Which rule does the ShopFlow monolith follow?
questions.explain: These are the layers from Backend architecture. Note the last option: that restriction is not enforced in the monolith, and its absence is what the modular monolith adds.
options: Every route writes its own SQL
SQL only in repositories, rules only in services, and everything created once in the composition root
Each area has its own database
Services may only call repositories of their own area

questions.q: What is the job of app.ts (createShop)?
questions.explain: The composition root is the one place that knows how the parts fit. Tests use it too, so they exercise the real wiring, and swapping the payment provider changes one argument.
options: Creating every part once and connecting them: repositories, services, the event bus and the router
Running the database migrations on every request

questions.q: What does SELECT … FOR UPDATE do in checkout?
questions.explain: The stock check and the stock update must not be interleaved with another checkout's. The row lock makes the second checkout wait, then read the updated stock. Plain reads without FOR UPDATE are not blocked.
options: Reads the rows and locks them until the transaction ends, so another checkout that wants the same rows waits
Prevents anyone from reading the table

questions.q: Why does lockForUpdate lock the product rows ORDER BY sku?
questions.explain: A deadlock needs two transactions each waiting for a lock the other holds: A holds rice and wants oil, B holds oil and wants rice. With one global order, both try rice first, so one simply waits for the other.
options: So the result is sorted for the customer
If every checkout locks rows in the same order, two checkouts can never each hold a row the other one is waiting for, which would be a deadlock
Because PostgreSQL requires it for FOR UPDATE

questions.q: Why is the card charged outside the transaction that reserves the stock?
questions.explain: Transactions must be short. The flow is reserve (short transaction), charge (no transaction), settle (short transaction). A slow provider then slows one customer, not every customer buying rice.
options: Because payments cannot be stored in PostgreSQL
A network call can take seconds; inside the transaction, the product rows would stay locked all that time and every other checkout for those products would queue
Because the provider needs the order to be committed first

questions.q: The card is declined after the stock was reserved. What does checkout do?
questions.explain: The reservation already committed, so it is undone by a second transaction, not by a rollback. Keeping the cancelled order (instead of deleting it) preserves the history of what happened.
options: Deletes the order and all its lines
In one transaction, puts the stock back and marks the order cancelled
Retries the card until it works

questions.q: Checkout passes order-<id> as the payment reference. What does that protect against?
questions.explain: The reference is the idempotency key from the adapters lesson. The order id is unique and known before the charge, which makes it a natural key.
options: Charging twice when the charge is retried after a timeout: the provider recognises the reference and returns the first result

questions.q: The lesson wraps the database so every transaction throws just before COMMIT. What does the test prove?
questions.explain: Simulating the failure at the worst moment is how you test atomicity. Every write inside the transaction is rolled back, so the database looks as if checkout never started.
options: That the order, its lines and the stock change are one unit: after the failure, none of them is saved

questions.q: Five checkouts for one bag of rice each run at the same time; three bags are in stock. What must happen?
questions.explain: With the lock, each checkout sees the stock the previous one left. The CHECK (stock >= 0) constraint is a second guard if the code were ever wrong.
options: All five succeed and the stock becomes -2
Exactly three succeed and two are refused; the stock ends at 0
All five are refused to be safe
The first succeeds and the others wait forever

questions.q: The oversell example runs on PGlite, which executes one transaction at a time. Does the result carry over to a PostgreSQL server with a connection pool?
questions.explain: PGlite happens to serialize, which hides the lock. A server needs the lock to get the same safety. That is why the code uses FOR UPDATE even though PGlite would pass without it; tests against a real server would catch its absence.
options: Yes: there the transactions really run in parallel, and FOR UPDATE makes the later ones wait for the row lock, giving the same result
Only if the pool has one connection
Only for products with stock above 10

questions.q: Ada, a customer, sends PUT /products/RICE-5KG with her valid token. Why does she get 403?
questions.explain: 401 would mean "we don't know who you are". 403 means "we know, and you may not". The role is put into the token by the server at login, from the database, never from the request.
options: The token's roles claim says customer, and the route's requireAdmin middleware refuses anyone who is not an admin
PUT is not allowed on products

questions.q: How does the monolith make sure nobody can sign up as an admin?
questions.explain: Anything in the request body is chosen by the client. Security-relevant fields such as roles must be set by the server.
options: The register route never reads a role from the request; register defaults to customer, and only code (a seed script or an admin) passes admin

questions.q: Why does checkout publish order.paid instead of calling the notifications service directly?
questions.explain: The in-process bus decouples the two parts inside one program. It is not durable, though: if the process dies right after the payment, the notification is lost. The outbox pattern fixes that when it matters.
options: Because direct calls are impossible in a monolith
Checkout then does not depend on notifications: new listeners can be added without changing checkout, and a failing handler does not fail the payment

questions.q: The orders repository's history query joins the products table. Why is that a strain as the shop grows?
questions.explain: In one database, reaching into another area's table is easy, and that is the problem: dependencies appear silently. The modular monolith makes orders ask the catalog through its public API, or store the product name it needs at checkout time.
options: The orders code now depends on the products table's structure; a rename or a move by the catalog team breaks orders, and nothing declared that dependency
Because products cannot be joined with orders in PostgreSQL
Because the query returns too many rows

questions.q: GET /notifications runs its SQL in the route. What is wrong with that?
questions.explain: One shortcut is harmless; a hundred are a big ball of mud. A "who uses what" check, like the one in the lesson, makes such shortcuts visible before they multiply.
options: It breaks the "SQL only in repositories" rule; every such shortcut spreads knowledge of tables into more places and makes the next change harder
It is slower than a repository

questions.q: On sale days the product pages get 100 times more traffic than checkout. What is the monolith's limitation here?
questions.explain: A monolith scales horizontally fine (run many copies behind a load balancer); it just cannot scale one part alone. Usually a cache or read replica solves read-heavy load long before a separate service is justified.
options: It cannot run more than one copy
It can only scale as a whole: to serve more product pages you run more copies of the entire shop, checkout included
Product pages must be moved to microservices at once

questions.q: ShopFlow runs as three copies behind a load balancer. Which part of this lesson's code must change first?
questions.explain: Anything kept in one process's memory that another copy needs breaks with several copies. The database is already shared, so the transaction and the constraints keep working.
options: The in-memory session store: a session created on one copy must be valid on the others, so sessions move to the database or Redis

questions.q: Three copies each open a connection pool of 10. The database allows 25 connections. What happens under load?
questions.explain: Pools are per process. The total is copies × pool size, and it must stay under the database's limit, with room for migrations and admin tools.
options: Nothing, pools share connections between copies
The copies together want 30 connections; some connection attempts fail or wait, so size pools against the database's limit

questions.q: Why must schema migrations in a monolith be done in backward-compatible steps?
questions.explain: Add a column, deploy code that writes both, backfill, switch reads, then remove the old column in a later deploy. One shared schema means one careless migration can break every area at once.
options: During a deploy, old and new copies run side by side against the same schema; a change that breaks the old code breaks the copies still serving traffic
Because migrations run in the browser

questions.q: A new image-resizing feature leaks memory until the process crashes. What is affected in the monolith?
questions.explain: Shared process, shared fate. This is one of the two strains only separate processes fix; the other is scaling parts independently. Code boundaries alone, as in a modular monolith, do not help here.
options: Everything, checkout included, because every feature runs in the same process

questions.q: Which strain does the modular monolith fix, while keeping one deployment?
questions.explain: Boundaries in the code and the data are an internal matter, so they can be enforced inside one program. Independent failure, scaling and release need separate processes.
options: A crash in one feature taking down all of them
Areas reaching into each other's tables and rules, because each module gets a public API and its own data

questions.q: How does checkout stay consistent in each architecture?
questions.explain: As long as the data is in one database, a transaction covers it, even with a schema per module. Once each service owns a separate database, no single transaction reaches across, and patterns replace it.
options: All three use one database transaction
Monolith and modular monolith: one transaction; microservices: sagas and outboxes, because each service has its own database
None of them can be consistent

questions.q: Three developers, 200 orders a day, weekly releases. The team lead wants to split ShopFlow into six services "to be ready for scale". What is the best answer?
questions.explain: Architecture should answer measured problems. Keep boundaries clean inside the monolith (which makes a later split mechanical) and revisit when a concrete reason appears.
options: Split now, it only gets harder later
Keep the monolith; none of the strains exists yet, and six services would add network failures, lost transactions and six deployments for no benefit
Rewrite it in another language first

questions.q: Checkout computes the total in kobo. What does this print?
questions.explain: Whole kobo add up exactly; converting to naira happens only for display. toFixed(2) keeps the two decimal places a price needs.

questions.q: This simulates the row lock with a promise chain. What does it print?
questions.explain: Each purchase waits for the previous one to finish before it reads the stock, like a transaction waiting for a row lock. Without withLock, all three would read 2 before any wrote, and all would "buy".
options:
[ 'Ada: bought', 'Bola: sold out', 'Chidi: sold out' ]
stock: 1

questions.q: The same code without the lock. What does it print?
questions.explain: All three read stock as 2 before any of them writes, so all three "buy", and each writes 1. Three bags sold from two, and the stock even claims one is left. This is the lost update that FOR UPDATE prevents.
options:
[ 'Ada: bought', 'Bola: sold out', 'Chidi: sold out' ]
stock: 1

questions.q: What does this notification text print?
questions.explain: Dividing by 100 turns kobo into naira; toLocaleString adds thousands separators and minimumFractionDigits: 2 keeps the kobo digits, even when they are zero.

questions.q: One order.paid handler fails. What does this print?
questions.explain: The bus runs every handler and reports the failure in the result instead of throwing, so the payment stays paid and the other listener still runs. Log result.errors; a failure nobody sees is a failure nobody fixes.

questions.q: Two checkouts lock their products in sorted order. What does this print?
questions.explain: Both carts want oil and rice, and both lock oil first. Whichever gets oil first also gets rice first; the other waits at oil while holding nothing, so no deadlock is possible.

questions.q: Checkout validates the cart before touching the database. What does this print?
questions.explain: Half a bag, an empty cart and a quantity sent as a string are all refused. [].every(…) is true, which is why the empty cart needs its own length > 0 check, and Number.isInteger("3") is false because strings are never converted.

questions.q: Write transaction(store, work) for an in-memory store (a Map): run work(copy) on a copy of the store; if it succeeds, copy the result back into the store; if it throws, leave the store unchanged and throw the error again.
questions.explain: If work throws, the lines that copy back never run, so the store keeps its old values: all or nothing. A database does the same with a log instead of a full copy, and also handles many transactions at once.

questions.q: Write reserve(stock, items): first check every item (unknown SKU: throw No product <sku>; too few: throw Only <n> of <sku> left), and only if all pass, take the quantities from stock. A refused cart must not change the stock at all.
questions.explain: Checking everything before changing anything keeps a refused cart harmless, even without a transaction. The lesson's checkout does both: it checks first, and the transaction protects against a failure in the middle of the writes.
questions.expected:
refused: Only 1 of OIL-1L left
RICE-5KG=3 OIL-1L=1
refused: No product SUGAR-1KG
RICE-5KG=3 OIL-1L=1
reserved
RICE-5KG=1 OIL-1L=0

questions.q: Write checkout(order, charge) in the reserve, charge, settle shape: reserve is done for you. Call await charge(order); on succeeded, return { status: "paid" }; on declined, call release(order) and return { status: "cancelled", reason }.
questions.explain: The declined order gives its stock back, so after two checkouts only the paid one has taken rice. In the real shop, reserve and release are each one short database transaction, and the charge sits between them with no transaction open.

questions.q: Given which area owns each table and which tables each file touches, print every use of a table owned by another area, as <file> uses <table> (owned by <area>).
questions.explain: Every printed line is a hidden dependency between areas. A monolith allows them; a modular monolith turns each into an explicit call to the owner's public API, or removes it.
questions.expected:
orders.repository.ts uses products (owned by products)
reports.service.ts uses orders (owned by orders)
reports.service.ts uses users (owned by users)

questions.q: Write httpStatus(error) for the shop's routes: use error.statusCode when it is a number from 400 to 599, otherwise 500. Then print the status for each error.
questions.explain: Errors from @zudojs/errors carry their status, so services throw ConflictError and the HTTP layer answers 409 without a try/catch in every route. Anything unknown, or with a nonsense status, is a 500 whose details stay in the logs.

questions.q: Build the order history lines the way the SQL history query does: for each order, join its lines with the product names, sort the items by product name, and print #<id> <status>: <quantity> x <name>, ….
questions.explain: This is the join done by hand. It also shows the dependency: to print a history line, the orders code needs the products' names. The modular monolith removes it by copying the name into the order line at checkout, so an order still says what the customer bought even if the product is renamed later.
questions.expected:
#1 paid: 1 x Palm oil 1L, 2 x Rice 5kg
#2 cancelled: 4 x Palm oil 1L
